title: Adjacent Spice Jars
story: A busy restaurant kitchen has one long shelf of spice jars. Each jar is labelled with one letter: c for cumin, p for paprika, s for salt, and so on. The shelf, read left to right, is a string like "sppcsx".

A recipe card lists the jars it needs, for example "cps". The chef wants to grab everything with one sweep of the arm: a block of jars standing side by side that holds exactly the recipe's jars, in any order, with nothing extra. Is there such a block on the shelf?
task: Write hasSpiceBlock(shelf, recipe). Return true if some run of recipe.length consecutive characters in shelf contains exactly the same letters as recipe, each the same number of times, in any order. Otherwise return false.
constraints: shelf and recipe contain lowercase letters a-z only.

examples.explanation: The first two blocks, spp and ppc, each have two p's. The block at positions 2 to 4, pcs, has one c, one p and one s: exactly the recipe, in a different order. Return true.
The recipe needs two a's and one p. The 3-jar blocks are pas, asp, spc, pca. None has two a's, even though the shelf has two a's in total. They are just too far apart.

hints: The block must have exactly recipe.length jars. In the first example that is 3. How many different 3-jar blocks does the shelf have, and how could you describe each one so the order does not matter?
Describe a block by how many jars of each letter it has. A block matches when its counts equal the recipe's counts.
Neighbouring blocks share all their jars but one at each end. When the block slides one step right, exactly one jar enters and one jar leaves, so you can update the counts instead of recounting.

Count the recipe's letters. Count the first m jars of the shelf (m = recipe length). Then slide: add the jar at i, remove the jar at i - m, and compare the two sets of counts after every step. With 26 letters, each comparison is a fixed amount of work.
bruteForce: For every starting position, take the next m jars, sort them, and compare with the sorted recipe.

Sorting each block costs about m log m. With a 10,000-jar shelf and a 1,000-letter recipe that is roughly 9,000 blocks × 10,000 steps: around 90 million operations. All that recounting is wasted, because each block differs from the previous one by just two jars.

py: def has_spice_block(shelf: str, recipe: str) -> bool:

js: const same = () => need.every((n, k) => n === have[k]);
for (let i = m; i < shelf.length; i++) {
have[idx(shelf[i])]++;      // jar entering on the right
have[idx(shelf[i - m])]--;  // jar leaving on the left
py: have[ord(shelf[i]) - 97] += 1      # jar entering on the right
have[ord(shelf[i - m]) - 97] -= 1  # jar leaving on the left
walkthrough: "Same jars in any order" means "same count of each letter". So describe the recipe by its letter counts, and keep the letter counts of a window of exactly m jars as it slides along the shelf.
Trace shelf "sppcsx" and recipe "cps", which needs c 1, p 1, s 1:
• First window spp: s 1, p 2. No c and one p too many. No match.
• Slide: c enters on the right, s leaves on the left. Window ppc: p 2, c 1. No match.
• Slide: s enters, p leaves. Window pcs: p 1, c 1, s 1. Same as the recipe. Return true.
Each slide changes exactly two counts, and comparing two arrays of 26 counts is a fixed amount of work, however long the recipe is.
solution.timeWhy: One pass over the shelf, and each step updates two counts and compares 26 numbers.
solution.spaceWhy: Two arrays of 26 counts, whatever the input size.
solution.takeaway: When order inside a window does not matter, describe the window by counts. A fixed-size window keeps those counts up to date with one add and one remove per step.
